title: ANOVA
body:
Three or more groups, and the question is whether their means differ:

$$
H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k
\qquad
H_1: \text{at least one differs}
$$

The obvious approach, running a two-sample $t$-test on every pair, is wrong. With $k = 5$ groups
that is $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ tests, and at $\alpha = 0.05$ each the chance of at least one false
positive is $1 - 0.95^{10} \approx 40\%$. **ANOVA is one test instead of ten, so the family-wise
error rate stays at $\alpha$.** That is its entire reason to exist, and it is the $p$-hacking
problem from [[P-VALUES]] solved properly rather than ignored.

## The idea, which the name gives away

You test means by looking at **variances**. If the groups really share a mean, then the spread
*between* the group means is just sampling noise, and it should look about the same size as the
spread *within* each group. If the groups differ, the between-group spread is inflated by the real
differences and the within-group spread is not.

$$
F = \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{between}}}{\text{MS}_{\text{within}}}
= \frac{\text{variance explained by group}}{\text{variance left over}}
$$

$F$ near 1 is consistent with $H_0$. $F$ large says the group labels explain more than chance. It is
always right-tailed, and it has two degrees-of-freedom parameters, $k-1$ on top and $n-k$ below.

## The decomposition

$$
\underbrace{\sum_{ij}(x_{ij} - \bar{x})^2}_{\text{SS}_{\text{total}}}
=
\underbrace{\sum_i n_i(\bar{x}_i - \bar{x})^2}_{\text{SS}_{\text{between}}}
+
\underbrace{\sum_{ij}(x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2}_{\text{SS}_{\text{within}}}
$$

Total variation splits exactly into explained plus unexplained, with degrees of freedom splitting
the same way: $(n-1) = (k-1) + (n-k)$. A mean square is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of
freedom, which is [[Variance]]'s $n-1$ rule generalised.

**This decomposition is the same one $r^2$ comes from in [[Correlation]]**, and it is the same
orthogonal split [[Least Squares]] in MATH 2303 calls Pythagoras: explained and residual are
perpendicular, so their squared lengths add. ANOVA, regression, and projection are three views of
one identity, and noticing that is worth more than memorising the table.

| Source | SS | df | MS | $F$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Between groups | $\text{SS}_B$ | $k-1$ | $\text{SS}_B/(k-1)$ | $\text{MS}_B/\text{MS}_W$ |
| Within groups | $\text{SS}_W$ | $n-k$ | $\text{SS}_W/(n-k)$ | |
| Total | $\text{SS}_T$ | $n-1$ | | |

## Conditions, and what comes after

Independent samples, roughly normal within each group, and **roughly equal variances across
groups**. The last one is the fragile assumption; ANOVA tolerates moderate violations, badly unequal
groups less so.

A significant $F$ says *some* pair differs and does not say which. Finding out needs a **post hoc**
procedure (Tukey, Bonferroni) that does the pairwise comparisons with the multiplicity correction
built in. Skipping straight to uncorrected $t$-tests after a significant $F$ puts back exactly the
error rate ANOVA was run to avoid.

With $k = 2$, ANOVA and the two-sample $t$-test are the same test, and $F = t^2$ exactly.

## Related
